questions.query: Why is regularization used when training a model?
questions.proposed_answer: Regularization reduces the risk of fitting the training data too closely and failing to generalize.

questions.query: What fitting problem does a complexity penalty help guard against?
questions.proposed_answer: Regularization reduces the risk of fitting the training data too closely and failing to generalize.

questions.query: What can happen when a model fits its training data without a complexity penalty?
questions.proposed_answer: Regularization reduces the risk of fitting the training data too closely and failing to generalize.

questions.query: Why should an ML model be tested on examples different from its training examples?
questions.proposed_answer: Held-out, nonduplicate examples provide a fairer and stronger test of whether predictions transfer beyond training cases.

questions.query: What makes unseen evaluation cases a stronger check than reusing the fitted cases?
questions.proposed_answer: Unseen cases test fitness beyond the examples the model already learned.

questions.query: Why is evaluating a model on the same records it learned from weak evidence of fitness?
questions.proposed_answer: Reusing training records is not a fair test of performance on genuinely new examples.

questions.query: What kind of response is regression intended to predict in the MIT lecture?
questions.proposed_answer: Regression predicts a real-valued continuous response for each example.

questions.query: What sort of target separates the regression setting described in the notes from label prediction?
questions.proposed_answer: The regression target is a continuous real-valued response rather than a discrete label.

questions.query: What two training distinctions are stated for logistic regression versus linear regression?
questions.proposed_answer: The lesson emphasizes Log Loss instead of squared loss and regularization to control overfitting. This does not mean linear regression cannot use regularization.

questions.query: Compared with linear regression, which loss and anti-overfitting measure does logistic regression use?
questions.proposed_answer: The lesson emphasizes Log Loss instead of squared loss and regularization to control overfitting. This does not mean linear regression cannot use regularization.

questions.query: Why should a linear-regression loss care about how far off a prediction is rather than whether it overshoots or undershoots?
questions.proposed_answer: Loss uses the magnitude of the prediction error, so the sign or direction of the error is removed.

questions.query: How do MSE and MAE differ in their sensitivity to outliers?
questions.proposed_answer: MSE squares errors and therefore pulls the model more strongly toward outliers; MAE is more robust to them.

questions.query: What steps does gradient descent repeat to reduce a linear model’s loss?
questions.proposed_answer: It evaluates the current loss, finds a loss-reducing direction, and moves the weights and bias a small amount in that direction repeatedly.

questions.query: What shape in a training loss curve indicates that gradient descent has converged?
questions.proposed_answer: Convergence is indicated when loss stops materially decreasing and the curve stabilizes or flattens.

questions.query: How do hyperparameters differ from model parameters?
questions.proposed_answer: A developer controls hyperparameters, while training calculates model parameters such as weights and bias.

questions.query: What training behavior suggests that the step size is too large?
questions.proposed_answer: An excessively high learning rate prevents convergence and makes loss bounce, fluctuate, or increase.

questions.query: What does one epoch mean during model training?
questions.proposed_answer: One epoch is completed when the model has processed every training example once.

questions.query: For finite real-valued inputs in the mathematical sigmoid, are 0 and 1 attained or only approached?
questions.proposed_answer: For finite real inputs in exact arithmetic, the output lies strictly between 0 and 1. The endpoints are approached as limits.

questions.query: What numerical-precision concern does the lesson give for squared loss near sigmoid outputs of 0 and 1?
questions.proposed_answer: Near 0 or 1, squared loss would require increasing numerical precision and memory to track small output differences.

questions.query: For scores strictly above or below a binary classification threshold, which class is assigned?
questions.proposed_answer: A score above the threshold is assigned to the positive class; a score below it to the negative class. Equality is outside this question and depends on the implementation.

questions.query: Why is 0.5 not automatically a sensible decision cutoff for every binary classifier?
questions.proposed_answer: A 0.5 cutoff can be inappropriate when classes are imbalanced or the two kinds of classification error have unequal costs.

questions.query: Why can accuracy be misleading on a heavily imbalanced dataset?
questions.proposed_answer: A model can predict only the majority class and earn very high accuracy while failing to identify the rare class at all.

questions.query: How could a useless always-negative classifier still report 99% correct predictions?
questions.proposed_answer: If positives are only 1% of examples, always predicting the majority negative class yields 99% accuracy despite no useful detection.

questions.query: In binary classification, what share of cases does sensitivity, also called recall, measure?
questions.proposed_answer: Recall is the fraction of all actual positives that the model correctly classifies as positive.

questions.query: What is precision in a binary classification evaluation?
questions.proposed_answer: Precision is the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive.

questions.query: Why does raising a classification cutoff often improve precision while hurting recall?
questions.proposed_answer: A higher threshold usually reduces false positives but increases false negatives, so precision and recall tend to move in opposite directions.

questions.query: How is an ROC curve constructed?
questions.proposed_answer: An ROC curve plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across threshold choices.

questions.query: What probability does AUC represent for a randomly selected positive-negative pair?
questions.proposed_answer: AUC is the probability that the model ranks the randomly selected positive example above the randomly selected negative example.

questions.query: In pairwise ranking terms, how should an AUC score be interpreted?
questions.proposed_answer: It measures how often a random positive receives a higher score than a random negative.

questions.query: In these learning examples, what numerical representation is used for one data instance?
questions.proposed_answer: A numeric feature vector, represented as an array or column vector of the example's feature values.

questions.query: What is feature engineering in the context of feature vectors?
questions.proposed_answer: Feature engineering is the process of turning raw dataset values into representations that a model can learn from.

questions.query: In the lesson's training example, why should numerical features with very different ranges be scaled?
questions.proposed_answer: Scaling prevents wide-range features from receiving disproportionate attention relative to narrow-range features.

questions.query: Why might the learner in the example initially treat a wider-range input as more important?
questions.proposed_answer: Without normalization, the model may treat the wider-range feature as more important solely because of its scale.

questions.query: When is Z-score scaling a good normalization choice?
questions.proposed_answer: Z-score scaling is well suited to normally or approximately normally distributed features.

questions.query: For what kind of distribution is log scaling helpful?
questions.proposed_answer: Log scaling is helpful for power-law or otherwise heavily skewed feature distributions.

thoroughly on the ideal regularization rate.

Epochs

During training, an epoch means that the
model has processed every example in the training set once. For example, given
a training set with 1,000 examples and a mini-batch size of 100 examples, it
will take the model 10 iterations to
complete one epoch.

Training typically requires many epochs. That is, the system needs to process
every example in the training set multiple times.

The number of epochs is a hyperparameter you set before the model begins
training. In many cases, you'll need to experiment with how many epochs it takes
for the model to converge. In general, more epochs produces a better model, but
also takes more time to train.
